claims.text: A cache stampede is many requests missing the same key at the same moment, usually just after it expired, so each sends the same query to the database at once.
ProductCache stores product:{id} with Ttl = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), so a stored copy lives 5 minutes unless deleted first.
new SemaphoreSlim(1, 1) has an initial and maximum count of 1: one caller holds it at a time; others waiting in WaitAsync continue only after Release() is called.
claims.source_hint: .NET API docs: SemaphoreSlim(int initialCount, int maxCount), SemaphoreSlim.Release

claims.text: await semaphore.WaitAsync() waits asynchronously to enter: the returned Task completes when the caller is let through, and no thread is blocked while it waits.
claims.source_hint: .NET API docs: SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync ('Asynchronously waits to enter the SemaphoreSlim')

claims.text: Without the per-key SemaphoreSlim, each of N concurrent misses would query PostgreSQL once and write Redis once; each miss also costs Redis GETs and a SET on top of the one query a read with no cache costs.
claims.source_hint: ProductCache.cs:25-49 @ stage-2 minus lines 31-39; cache-aside lesson claim 19

claims.text: Stampede size depends on how many requests arrive for the key while it is missing (from the key disappearing until the first request stores it again), not on the size of the cached value; later requests are hits.

FindAsync: GetAsync; a hit returns before any SemaphoreSlim code. On a miss: Locks.GetOrAdd(key, _ => new SemaphoreSlim(1, 1)), await WaitAsync(), second GetAsync (hit returns), else inner.FindAsync + SetAsync if not null; Release() in finally. inner is the EfProductRepository.
Locks is a static ConcurrentDictionary<string, SemaphoreSlim> (comment: one per key, shared by every request in this api process); ProductCache itself is registered scoped, a new one per request.

ConcurrentDictionary<TKey,TValue> is a thread-safe collection many threads can use at once. GetOrAdd(key, valueFactory) returns the existing value or adds one; concurrent callers for one key all get the same stored object.
A finally block runs whenever control leaves the try block: after a return inside try or when an exception is thrown in it.

Via scripts/up.sh (Compose) the API runs as one container (service api, container_name donhang-api); deploy/k8s/api.yaml runs 2 replicas, each a separate process with its own memory and its own static Locks.

With one API process, a product that exists and Redis answering, an expired key costs one query; with two API copies sharing Redis, up to one per copy (two). A missing product or Redis error makes each waiter query in turn.

cache-stampede.sh runs on the host: redis DEL product:3 ('as if its TTL had just run out'), then 20 GET /api/v1/products/3 sent at once with curl --parallel, then counts 'FROM products' lines in docker compose logs of api.

EF Core logs each SQL command it sends under Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command at Information; appsettings.json keeps EF Core at Warning, and the lab docker-compose.yml raises that category for api.
claims.source_hint: EF Core docs: Simple logging / CommandExecuted; docker-compose.yml:124-127 @ stage-2

claims.text: Script output at stage-2: all 20 requests answered 200, and PostgreSQL ran 1 products query for them.
UpdatePriceAsync deletes product:{id} from Redis after a successful price update, which makes the next reads misses just like an expiry.
A longer TTL makes expiries rarer but does not stop the moment a popular key is missing; the rush size depends on requests arriving then, not on how long the key lived.
Running cache-stampede.sh twice prints 1 query both times, because each run deletes product:3 before sending the requests.
